name: Data-Driven UX Improvement
description: Led the usability process from research to client delivery, improving website performance and accessibility by 48%

goal.headline: The client wanted a faster, more accessible site
body: It wasn't that simple: the site wasn't just an e-commerce platform, it was also a hub for scientific articles. The redesign had to balance dense information, reading comfort, and enough visual polish that the client felt the investment was worth it, without breaking the site's original purpose.

priorities.headline: What did the client actually need to fix first?
body: I collaborated with my manager and the project manager to build a survey sent to 25 employees and executives to surface goals, pain points, competitive positioning, and visual direction.
Three priorities came out on top:

setup.headline: I built a usability test around those three priorities
body: The client worked in antibody synthesis, a scientific field, so a data-driven approach mattered for getting buy-in from decision makers. I scoped the test around the three priorities: purchase, information sharing, and lead generation, then split it into a task-based stage and a SUS stage to capture both quantitative and qualitative signal.

Five moderated sessions, enough to surface the majority of core usability issues, gave me completion rate, time on task, error count, click count, navigation style, and subjective satisfaction for each task. I combined those into a weighted efficiency score per task.

findings.headline: Buying was fine. Everything else wasn't
body: Purchasing was relatively efficient, though click count was higher than it should be. The real problem sat in the secondary goals: article search and lead generation both saw significant abandonment. The SUS results pointed to a site that felt unnecessarily complex to navigate, even though reading quality got positive feedback.

categories.headline: I organized every finding into six categories
body: Qualitative, quantitative, behavioral, technical, user-journey, and accessibility. Each observation, from SUS sentiment to task data to video-based behavior patterns, was paired with a potential design fix.

fixes.headline: Every insight had to be paired with an actual design
body: So the impact was undeniable. I filtered the findings down to what mattered most against the client's original priorities, then matched each one to a concrete design change:
list: Smarter use of space to shorten pages
Eye-catching sections built specifically for lead generation and contact
Dynamic content loading on scroll and tabs to speed up initial load
A sticky side panel to guide navigation toward key sections and products
Accessibility fixes to color contrast and font sizing, flagged directly against the site's PSI score
body2: The redesign also extended into a full Design System refresh: new typography, colors, icons, and components.

trust.headline: The client didn't trust user sessions as proof
body: So we brought in a score they did trust: the PageSpeed Insights (PSI) report, showing that specific choices like undersized text and weak color contrast weren't just usability issues, they were actively hurting the site's accessibility score. Showing the 90+ score within reach was what finally got their buy-in.

feedback.headline: Every round of feedback multiplied into more back-and-forth
body: To answer this, the PM and I decided to give them pieces to build with instead: static snapshots of individual Design System components, buttons, tabs, cards, letting the client assemble the exact layout they had in mind and turning the conversation into specifics instead of abstractions. Revision rounds dropped from 8 to 2.

direction.headline: Client wanted to stay classic, but the data said otherwise
body: I proposed two design directions: one brand-forward and bold, one closer to the existing classic, information-dense layout. The client's instinct leaned toward the safer, classic option, but working with the project manager, we made the case for the bolder direction instead, using the audience age data from GA4 to show it was the better fit. They went with it.

impact.headline: I selected the four insights most likely to move the needle
body: Not everything made the cut. Out of the full set of findings, I chose the four with the clearest link to the original priorities, the ones that would fix lead generation and resource navigation directly. The client stayed aligned with those priorities throughout, satisfaction was high, and it opened the door to additional phases of work.

list.title: Automate user behavior analysis
list.body: Behavioral data was hand-logged from session recordings. It was accurate, but used three days of work for five users. For future tests, I would provide automated tracking tools so quantitative data come out more quickly and accurately.

list.title: Challenge decisions that we knew wouldn't grow
list.body: We let the client steer toward a layout that looked right short-term but wasn't scalable, and phase two is now patching around it. Since then, I introduced a version system so future adjustments build on the structure instead of overwriting it.

list.title: Flag the unproductive feedback pace earlier
list.body: Revisions came in unpredictably, one-off change a day, large batches the next, which harmed the design system's scalability over time. I now set explicit feedback-cadence expectations with the PM upfront.
